Elizabeth Báthory was accused of burning young women in her service with hot irons.
Of forcing others into freezing water.
People said young women were dying in her household.
The rumours reached the king.
He sent Hungary's highest official, György Thurzó, to investigate.
One December night, armed men arrived at her manor.
Báthory was eating supper.
Thurzó wrote that his men had found one girl dead and another dying of her wounds.
Báthory was taken to the fortress above her home.
Four of her servants, three women and a young man, were arrested as her alleged accomplices.
Under torture, they confessed to dozens of killings.
Three were executed within days.
But Báthory was never tried.
The king pressed for a trial.
Thurzó prevented it.
Her powerful family wanted no public trial.
And many witnesses could only repeat what they had heard.
She died in confinement.
Then someone added the detail that would make her infamous.
More than a century after her death, a priest wrote that she bathed in murdered girls' blood to keep her beauty.
No witness against her had described that.
No court ever heard her.
But the legend had its monster:
the Blood Countess.
<break time="0.8s"/> History remembers the victors.
We remember the rest.
